--- title: "SQLEquiv: A Multi-Method Library for SQL Query Equivalence Analysis" subtitle: "Algebraic, Graph-Based, and Embedding-Based Approaches" author: - name: Yifan Yang email: yfyang.86@hotmail.com affiliation: Open NL2SQL / Chat2BI course (2025-Dec) date: last-modified abstract: | We present **SQLEquiv**, an open-source Python library that decides SQL query equivalence through three complementary lenses: rule-based relational-algebra rewriting, NetworkX-backed graph isomorphism with a weighted structural-similarity fallback, and cosine similarity over deterministic vector embeddings. A single unified analyzer dispatches to the three methods and reports a unanimous verdict together with per-method confidences. The paper formalizes what each method computes, details the software architecture, and works through a reproducible battery of examples — from textbook cases to queries with CTEs, window functions, set operations, and nested subqueries. We close with a documented set of known gaps and a forward-looking roadmap. keywords: - SQL equivalence - relational algebra - graph isomorphism - query embeddings - reproducible research bibliography: references.bib format: html: toc: true toc-depth: 3 number-sections: true code-tools: true code-fold: show theme: cosmo highlight-style: github pdf: toc: true number-sections: true documentclass: article geometry: - margin=1in execute: echo: true warning: false error: false cache: false jupyter: python3 --- # Introduction {#sec-intro} Deciding whether two SQL queries are **equivalent** — i.e. produce the same result for every database instance — is a foundational problem at the intersection of databases, programming languages, and modern NL2SQL tooling. In general, equivalence of SQL with aggregation, NULL semantics, and duplicates is undecidable [@cosette2017], so practical systems combine conservative decision procedures (sound but incomplete) with heuristic similarity measures. **SQLEquiv** is a modest open-source step in that direction. It exposes a single `SQLEquivalenceAnalyzer` that runs three independent methods and reports both a unanimous verdict and per-method confidences: 1. **Algebraic** — canonicalize each query into a relational-algebra expression tree and compare, driven by a fixed set of rewrite rules (selection / projection pushdown, join commutativity and associativity, union commutativity, etc.). 2. **Graph** — materialize a directed attribute graph from the query's abstract syntax tree (AST) and run attribute-aware isomorphism, falling back to a weighted structural-similarity cascade when isomorphism fails. 3. **Embedding** — produce a deterministic vector per query (either via node-feature pooling over the graph, or a pluggable `encode`-bearing model such as the built-in `HashingVectorEncoder`) and score with cosine similarity mapped to $[0, 1]$. The library targets Python 3.8+ and builds on [`sqlglot`](https://github.com/tobymao/sqlglot) for dialect-robust parsing. This manuscript is a Quarto [@quarto2022] document so every code block is executed at render time — readers can reproduce every number, table, and figure below with the commands in @sec-reproducing. # Theory {#sec-theory} ## Problem statement Given two queries $q_1, q_2$ over a common database schema $\mathcal{D}$, write $[\![ q ]\!]_D$ for the multiset of rows returned by $q$ on instance $D \in \mathcal{D}$. Two notions of equivalence are useful: $$ \begin{aligned} q_1 \equiv_{\text{set}} q_2 &\iff \forall D.\ \operatorname{set}[\![ q_1 ]\!]_D = \operatorname{set}[\![ q_2 ]\!]_D \\ q_1 \equiv_{\text{bag}} q_2 &\iff \forall D.\ [\![ q_1 ]\!]_D = [\![ q_2 ]\!]_D \end{aligned} $$ Set-equivalence ignores duplicates; bag-equivalence preserves multiplicities. The two differ on `UNION` vs `UNION ALL`, `SELECT` vs `SELECT DISTINCT`, and any rewrite that duplicates or collapses tuples. SQLEquiv's algebraic checker targets bag-equivalence up to the supported rules; the graph and embedding checkers are structural heuristics that do not strictly decide either notion. ## Algebraic method The algebraic method compiles each query to a relational-algebra expression tree. We use the standard operator set $\{\pi, \sigma, \bowtie, \cup, \cap, -, \gamma, \tau, \delta\}$ [@silberschatz2019; @garcia2008]: projection, selection, natural / theta join, union, intersect, difference, aggregation, sort, and distinct. The checker then tests equivalence in three phases: 1. **Identity** — direct structural equality $T_1 \stackrel{?}{=} T_2$ on the operator trees. 2. **Normalization** — rewrite each tree to a canonical form using idempotent transformations (@eq-selection-pushdown, @eq-join-commutativity) and retest identity. 3. **Transformation search** — bounded DFS over the rewrite rules attempting to transform $T_1$ into $T_2$ within a configurable depth limit. Selection pushdown: $$ \sigma_p(R \bowtie S) \equiv \begin{cases} \sigma_{p_R}(R) \bowtie \sigma_{p_S}(S) & \text{if } p = p_R \wedge p_S,\\ \sigma_{p_R}(R) \bowtie S & \text{if } p \text{ touches only } R,\\ R \bowtie \sigma_{p_S}(S) & \text{if } p \text{ touches only } S. \end{cases} $$ {#eq-selection-pushdown} Join commutativity (inner join only): $$ R \bowtie S \equiv S \bowtie R. $$ {#eq-join-commutativity} When none of the phases produces a match, the checker returns a soft similarity in $[0, 1]$ built from operator-type distribution, tree structure, shared tables, and shared predicates. ## Graph method Every query is converted into a labeled directed graph $G = (V, E, \ell_V, \ell_E)$ where vertices correspond to AST nodes, edges encode parent-child AST relationships, and label functions $\ell_V, \ell_E$ carry `(type, value, attributes)` dictionaries. Two attribute-aware matchers are used: $$ \begin{aligned} \mu_V(u, v) &= [\ell_V(u).\text{type} = \ell_V(v).\text{type}] \cdot [\ell_V(u).\text{value} = \ell_V(v).\text{value}] \\ \mu_E(e_1, e_2) &= [\ell_E(e_1).\text{type} = \ell_E(e_2).\text{type}] \end{aligned} $$ Exact equivalence is reported when `networkx.is_isomorphic` returns true under $(\mu_V, \mu_E)$ [@hagberg2008]. Otherwise the checker computes a weighted similarity $$ \operatorname{sim}_G(G_1, G_2) \;=\; \sum_{k \in \{\text{node}, \text{edge}, \text{struct}, \text{spec}\}} w_k \cdot s_k(G_1, G_2), $$ {#eq-graph-sim} with weights $w = (0.3, 0.3, 0.2, 0.2)$ and components: - $s_{\text{node}}$ — blend of a Jaccard over the node-type histogram and a Jaccard over the `(type, value)` histogram (so a different table name actually lowers the score). - $s_{\text{edge}}$ — Jaccard over the edge-type histogram. - $s_{\text{struct}}$ — $1 - \lVert \vec{d}_1 - \vec{d}_2 \rVert_2 / (\lVert \vec{d}_1 \rVert_2 + \lVert \vec{d}_2 \rVert_2)$ on sorted degree sequences. - $s_{\text{spec}}$ — same shape applied to Laplacian spectra. The configurable threshold (default 0.9) maps @eq-graph-sim to an `APPROXIMATE` verdict. For a hard distance, the library also exposes `compute_graph_edit_distance`, a wall-clock-bounded call to NetworkX's `optimize_graph_edit_distance` [@abu2015; @riesen2009]. ## Embedding method Given a graph $G$ and a per-node encoder $f_\theta: \mathcal{V} \to \mathbb{R}^d$, a pooled query vector is $$ \vec{v}(q) = \rho\big(\{f_\theta(n)\}_{n \in V}\big), $$ with $\rho$ one of mean / sum / max pooling. The library ships two built-in encoders: 1. `NodeEmbedding` — deterministic pseudo-random vectors seeded by a stable hash of each node's `(type, name)` key. 2. `HashingVectorEncoder` — a hashing-trick encoder [@weinberger2009] over the SQL text itself with optional n-gram features; zero-extra-dependency and reproducible. Third-party models (GNNs, pretrained code LMs) plug in by exposing a single `encode(query) -> np.ndarray` method. Similarity is cosine, clipped and rescaled to $[0, 1]$: $$ \operatorname{sim}_E(q_1, q_2) = \max\!\bigg(0,\; \min\!\bigg(1,\; \frac{1 + \cos\big(\vec{v}(q_1), \vec{v}(q_2)\big)}{2}\bigg)\bigg). $$ {#eq-cosine} ## Combining methods The analyzer runs each requested method and records per-method `{is_equivalent, confidence, equivalence_type}`. The headline verdict is **unanimous-agreement** — `is_equivalent` is true only when every method votes yes. The aggregate confidence is the fraction of yes votes, so disagreement surfaces as a fractional score. This policy is documented in `Future-Plan.md` as an open design question; callers who prefer weighted or short-circuit voting can compose their own logic over `AnalysisResult.method_results`. # Software architecture {#sec-architecture} The package is organised into seven subsystems: | Subsystem | Files | Responsibility | |---|---|---| | Parser | `parser/sql_parser.py`, `parser/ast_builder.py`, `parser/normalizer.py` | `sqlglot` → `ParsedQuery` + `ASTNode` tree. | | Representations | `representations/algebraic/*`, `representations/graph/*`, `representations/embedding/*` | Algebraic trees, query graphs, logical query trees, vector encoders. | | Equivalence | `equivalence/algebraic_equivalence.py`, `equivalence/graph_equivalence.py`, `equivalence/embedding_similarity.py` | One `EquivalenceChecker` per method. | | Operators | `operators/*.py` | SELECT / FROM / JOIN / aggregate / window / scalar operator classes. | | Transformations | `transformations/algebraic_rules.py`, `transformations/graph_transformations.py`, `transformations/optimization_rules.py` | Rewrite rules consumed by the checkers. | | Analyzer | `analyzer.py`, `plugins.py`, `proof_export.py` | Public entry point, plugin registry, Markdown/JSON proof export. | | Utils | `utils/*.py`, `models/embedding_models.py` | SQL / graph / algebra helpers, `HashingVectorEncoder`. | ## Plugin registry Custom analysis methods are registered either at runtime or through the `sql_equivalence.methods` entry-point group. The plugin contract is a single callable `(parsed_query_1, parsed_query_2, detailed: bool) -> dict` that returns at minimum `is_equivalent`, `confidence`, and `equivalence_type`. Built-in methods are themselves registered this way, so there is a single dispatch table. ## Dependency policy The core install depends only on `sqlglot`, `networkx`, `numpy`, `scipy`, `scikit-learn`, and `pandas`. Heavy visualization dependencies (`graphviz`, `plotly`) are imported lazily inside the functions that need them; the optional `[ml]` extra is reserved for plugin-authored learned encoders. # Installation and reproducibility {#sec-install} ```bash # Core install (no GPU / visualization deps) pip install sql-equivalence # Optional extras pip install "sql-equivalence[viz]" # matplotlib + graphviz + plotly pip install "sql-equivalence[ml]" # torch + transformers (plugin targets) pip install "sql-equivalence[dev]" # pytest + ruff + mypy # From source (developer mode) git clone https://github.com/yfyang86/SQLEquiv cd SQLEquiv pip install -e "sql_equivalence[dev]" ``` To render this manuscript: ```bash pip install -e . # or: pip install sql-equivalence quarto render manuscript/main.qmd --to html # or --to pdf ``` # Examples and simulations {#sec-examples} All examples in this section are live Python blocks — the numbers below are produced by the current library at render time. ## Setting up ::: {#setup .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import logging, warnings logging.disable(logging.CRITICAL) # silence library chatter warnings.filterwarnings("ignore") import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sql_equivalence import SQLEquivalenceAnalyzer from sql_equivalence.models import HashingVectorEncoder from sql_equivalence.proof_export import to_markdown analyzer = SQLEquivalenceAnalyzer() print("Available methods:", analyzer.available_methods) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Available methods: ('algebraic', 'embedding', 'graph') ``` ::: ::: ## Identical queries ::: {#identical .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} sql = "SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE age >= 18" result = analyzer.analyze(sql, sql) print(f"Verdict: {result.is_equivalent} (confidence {result.confidence:.2f})") for method, outcome in result.method_results.items(): print(f" {method}: eq={outcome['is_equivalent']} " f"conf={outcome['confidence']:.3f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Verdict: True (confidence 1.00) algebraic: eq=True conf=1.000 graph: eq=True conf=1.000 embedding: eq=True conf=1.000 ``` ::: ::: ## Structurally different queries ::: {.cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} pairs = [ ("Same query, different DB table", "SELECT id FROM users", "SELECT id FROM customers"), ("Plain vs aggregated", "SELECT id FROM t", "SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM emp GROUP BY dept HAVING COUNT(*) > 1"), ("Extra JOIN", "SELECT a.id FROM a JOIN b ON a.id = b.aid JOIN c ON b.cid = c.id", "SELECT a.id FROM a JOIN b ON a.id = b.aid"), ] rows = [] for name, q1, q2 in pairs: r = analyzer.analyze(q1, q2) rows.append({ "case": name, "overall_is_equivalent": r.is_equivalent, "confidence": round(r.confidence, 3), "algebraic": r.method_results["algebraic"]["is_equivalent"], "graph": r.method_results["graph"]["is_equivalent"], "embedding": r.method_results["embedding"]["is_equivalent"], }) pd.DataFrame(rows) ``` ::: {#different .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
case overall_is_equivalent confidence algebraic graph embedding
0 Same query, different DB table False 0.667 True False True
1 Plain vs aggregated False 0.000 False False False
2 Extra JOIN False 0.667 True False True
``` ::: ::: ## Common Table Expressions ::: {#cte .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} cte1 = ("WITH adults AS (SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE age >= 18) " "SELECT id FROM adults") cte2 = ("WITH adults AS (SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE age >= 18) " "SELECT id FROM adults") print("Identical CTE:", analyzer.analyze(cte1, cte2).is_equivalent) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Identical CTE: True ``` ::: ::: ## Window functions ::: {#windows .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} w1 = ("SELECT id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) " "AS rn FROM emp") w2 = ("SELECT id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) " "AS rn FROM emp") r = analyzer.analyze(w1, w2) print(f"Identical window fn: eq={r.is_equivalent} conf={r.confidence:.2f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Identical window fn: eq=True conf=1.00 ``` ::: ::: ## Known gaps The following cases are deliberately tracked as `xfail(strict=True)` regression markers in `sql_equivalence/tests/fixtures.py::KNOWN_GAP_PAIRS`. The analyzer currently returns **equivalent** for each; tightening any entry here requires the corresponding checker rule to be tightened. ::: {.cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} gaps = [ ("Opposite WHERE", "SELECT id FROM users WHERE age > 10", "SELECT id FROM users WHERE age < 10"), ("INNER vs LEFT JOIN", "SELECT a.id FROM a INNER JOIN b ON a.id = b.aid", "SELECT a.id FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.id = b.aid"), ("UNION vs UNION ALL", "SELECT id FROM a UNION SELECT id FROM b", "SELECT id FROM a UNION ALL SELECT id FROM b"), ("LIMIT 10 vs LIMIT 100", "SELECT id FROM t LIMIT 10", "SELECT id FROM t LIMIT 100"), ("COUNT vs SUM", "SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM emp GROUP BY dept", "SELECT dept, SUM(salary) FROM emp GROUP BY dept"), ] pd.DataFrame([ {"case": n, "overall_is_equivalent": analyzer.analyze(a, b).is_equivalent} for n, a, b in gaps ]) ``` ::: {#known-gaps .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ```{=html}
case overall_is_equivalent
0 Opposite WHERE True
1 INNER vs LEFT JOIN True
2 UNION vs UNION ALL True
3 LIMIT 10 vs LIMIT 100 True
4 COUNT vs SUM True
``` ::: ::: ## Custom analysis method (plugin) ::: {#plugin .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} from sql_equivalence import plugins def identical_text_only(parsed1, parsed2, detailed): eq = parsed1.sql.strip() == parsed2.sql.strip() return { "is_equivalent": eq, "confidence": 1.0 if eq else 0.0, "equivalence_type": "exact" if eq else "not_equivalent", } plugins.unregister_method("text_eq") analyzer.register_method("text_eq", identical_text_only) r = analyzer.analyze( "SELECT id FROM t", "select id from t", methods=["text_eq"], ) print("Plugin vote:", r.method_results["text_eq"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Plugin vote: {'is_equivalent': False, 'confidence': 0.0, 'equivalence_type': 'not_equivalent'} ``` ::: ::: ## Custom embedding model ::: {#embedding .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} encoder = HashingVectorEncoder(dim=128, ngram_range=(1, 2)) analyzer_custom = SQLEquivalenceAnalyzer(embedding_model=encoder) r = analyzer_custom.analyze( "SELECT id, name FROM users", "select id , name from users", methods=["embedding"], ) print(f"Whitespace/case only: sim={r.method_results['embedding']['confidence']:.3f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Whitespace/case only: sim=1.000 ``` ::: ::: ## Batch analysis ::: {.cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} batch = [ ("SELECT id FROM t", "SELECT id FROM t"), ("SELECT id FROM users", "SELECT id FROM customers"), ("SELECT * FROM a", "SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM emp GROUP BY dept"), ] results = analyzer.batch_analyze(batch) pd.DataFrame([ {"sql1": r.sql1, "sql2": r.sql2, "is_equivalent": r.is_equivalent, "confidence": round(r.confidence, 3)} for r in results ]) ``` ::: {#batch .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ```{=html}
sql1 sql2 is_equivalent confidence
0 SELECT id FROM t SELECT id FROM t True 1.000
1 SELECT id FROM users SELECT id FROM customers False 0.667
2 SELECT * FROM a SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM emp GROUP BY dept False 0.000
``` ::: ::: ## Latency micro-benchmark A rough end-to-end latency profile on the shared fixture corpus (run on whatever machine renders this document): ::: {.cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} import statistics, time from sql_equivalence.tests.fixtures import EQUIVALENT_PAIRS, NON_EQUIVALENT_PAIRS CORPUS = list(EQUIVALENT_PAIRS) + list(NON_EQUIVALENT_PAIRS) samples_ms = [] bench_analyzer = SQLEquivalenceAnalyzer(enable_caching=False) for _ in range(10): for sql1, sql2 in CORPUS: t = time.perf_counter() bench_analyzer.analyze(sql1, sql2) samples_ms.append((time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000.0) pd.DataFrame([{ "pairs": len(CORPUS), "runs": 10, "min_ms": round(min(samples_ms), 2), "mean_ms": round(statistics.mean(samples_ms), 2), "median_ms": round(statistics.median(samples_ms), 2), "max_ms": round(max(samples_ms), 2), }]) ``` ::: {#bench .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ```{=html}
pairs runs min_ms mean_ms median_ms max_ms
0 11 10 1.56 2.75 2.69 4.42
``` ::: ::: ## Proof export ::: {#proof .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} r = analyzer.analyze( "SELECT id FROM t", "SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM emp GROUP BY dept HAVING COUNT(*) > 1", methods=["algebraic"], detailed=True, ) print(to_markdown(r)[:1200]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ```` # SQL equivalence analysis **Verdict**: NOT EQUIVALENT (confidence 0.000) **Execution time**: 8.23 ms ## Queries ```sql -- Q1 SELECT id FROM t ``` ```sql -- Q2 SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM emp GROUP BY dept HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 ``` ## Per-method results - ❌ **algebraic** — type=not_equivalent, confidence=0.500 - `canonical_form1`: π[*](unknown) - `canonical_form2`: π[*](σ[{}](G[](unknown))) ```` ::: ::: # Reproducing the manuscript {#sec-reproducing} The entire document is an executable Quarto notebook. To reproduce: ```bash # 1. Install the library and manuscript dependencies pip install sql-equivalence quarto-cli jupyter pandas # 2. Render the manuscript to HTML or PDF quarto render manuscript/main.qmd --to html quarto render manuscript/main.qmd --to pdf # requires LaTeX ``` Every numeric value and every table in @sec-examples is produced by the live code blocks at render time. The corpus lives in `sql_equivalence/tests/fixtures.py`; swapping in a larger corpus is a one-line edit. # Limitations and future work {#sec-limitations} SQLEquiv is an alpha-stage library and the known gaps listed in @sec-examples are real. The algebraic checker in particular is too lenient on column-name and predicate-direction differences because its canonical form collapses to a `Project(*, Relation(t))` scaffold when AST traversal bottoms out. Tightening requires: (i) projection column-list comparison, (ii) predicate-sign aware normalization, and (iii) multiplicity-aware rules for `UNION` vs `UNION ALL` and `DISTINCT`. The graph similarity weights are set by hand; learning them from a labeled corpus is an obvious avenue for future work. Scope boundaries that we do **not** plan to cross are spelled out in `Future-Plan.md`: we will not ship a custom SQL parser (sqlglot is the source of truth), we will not execute queries against a live database to sample equivalence, and we will not grow the default install with GPU-dependent models. Anything richer belongs in a plugin package. # Acknowledgements {.unnumbered} The library is part of the open NL2SQL / Chat2BI course (2025-Dec). SQL parsing is carried by `sqlglot` [@sqlglot]; graph algorithms use `networkx` [@hagberg2008]; embeddings leverage `numpy` and `scikit-learn`. # References {.unnumbered} ::: {#refs} :::
